claims.claim: Le Guin says narrative prose going a long distance needs more muscle than fat, and recommends a thoughtful, careful choice of adjectives and adverbs.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)

claims.claim: Le Guin's Chastity exercise asks the writer to produce descriptive narrative prose without adjectives or adverbs, using only verbs, nouns, pronouns and articles.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)

claims.claim: Le Guin says the word suddenly seldom means anything at all and is a mere transition device.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: Suddenly seldom means anything at all

claims.claim: Le Guin says stating flatly that repetition is to be avoided goes right against the nature of narrative prose.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: repetition is the central means of achieving rhythm

claims.claim: In Le Guin's detached-author point of view, people and places may be exactly described but values and judgments can only be implied indirectly.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: values and judgments can only be implied indirectly
claims.page: chapter 7, 'Point of View and Voice', Detached Author

claims.claim: Le Guin says that in the detached-author point of view the author never enters a character's mind.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: The author never enters a character’s mind.
claims.page: chapter 7, 'Point of View and Voice', Detached Author

claims.claim: Le Guin calls the detached-author voice the least overtly and most covertly manipulative of the points of view.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: the least overtly, most covertly manipulative of the points of view
claims.page: chapter 7, 'Point of View and Voice', Detached Author

claims.claim: Le Guin says the world of a science fiction or fantasy story must be created and explained in the story, because the reader has no way of knowing it otherwise.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: must be created and explained in the story

claims.claim: Le Guin says crafty writers break information up, grind it fine, and make it into bricks to build the story with, rather than letting exposition form lumps.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: grind it fine, and make it into bricks

claims.claim: Le Guin says the story is not in the plot but in the telling, and that it is the telling that moves.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story (Mariner Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2015)
claims.quote: The story is not in the plot but in the telling.

claims.claim: Le Guin opens Steering the Craft by saying the sound of the language is where it all begins and that the test of a sentence is whether it sounds right.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'The Sound of Your Writing', chapter one of Steering the Craft (2015), excerpted at Literary Hub
claims.quote: The sound of the language is where it all begins.

claims.claim: Le Guin says pace and movement depend above all on rhythm, and that the primary way to feel and control the rhythm of prose is by hearing it.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'The Sound of Your Writing', chapter one of Steering the Craft (2015), excerpted at Literary Hub
claims.quote: Pace and movement depend above all on rhythm

claims.claim: Introducing a passage of Zora Neale Hurston, Le Guin says the vocabulary is simple and familiar and that it is above all the rhythm that is powerful and effective.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'The Sound of Your Writing', chapter one of Steering the Craft (2015), excerpted at Literary Hub
claims.quote: the vocabulary is simple and familiar
claims.page: chapter one, note introducing example III

claims.claim: Le Guin says the sound of the names of places can be intensely expressive, citing Faulkner's Yoknapatawpha County and Tolkien's simple yet deeply evocative Middle-earth.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'The Sound of Your Writing', chapter one of Steering the Craft (2015), excerpted at Literary Hub
claims.quote: his simple yet deeply evocative Middle-earth
claims.page: chapter one, 'to think or talk about afterward'

claims.feature: other: prose that stops to be admired
claims.claim: Le Guin asks whether a novelist who visibly strives for striking or poetical prose, using unusual or archaic words, intensifies what is being said or distracts from it.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'The Sound of Your Writing', chapter one of Steering the Craft (2015), excerpted at Literary Hub
